title: Dates vs. sugar: nutrition differences

seo.title: Dates vs. sugar: calories, sugar and fiber compared
seo.meta_description: Dates contain less sugar by weight and provide fiber, but they are still concentrated. Compare 100 g and equal-size portions to see the real difference.
seo.search_intent: Compare whole dates with table sugar and understand whether using dates for sweetness offers a meaningful nutritional advantage.

excerpt: Per 100 g, Medjool dates provide about 277 calories, 66–67 g of sugars and 6.7 g of fiber; granulated sugar has roughly 387 calories, 100 g of sugar and no fiber. At equal weight, dates contain less sugar and energy because they also contain water and fiber. That makes them a more complete food, not an unlimited sweetener: 20 g of dates still has about 55 calories and 13 g of sugars.
content_html:
Blended dates can sweeten oatmeal, energy bites, sauces, or baked goods, which is why they are often presented as a “natural sugar replacement.” Natural does not tell you how much sweetness ends up in the food. The more useful distinction is that a date is concentrated whole fruit, while table sugar is nearly pure sucrose.

Gram for gram, dates look quite different

One hundred grams of Medjool dates contains about 277 calories, 66–67 g of sugars, and 6.7 g of fiber. One hundred grams of granulated sugar contains roughly 387 calories, 100 g of sugar, and 0 g of fiber. Dates also contribute potassium and smaller amounts of other minerals.

Per 100 gMedjool datesGranulated sugar
Energy≈277 kcal≈387 kcal
Sugars≈66–67 g≈100 g
Fiber≈6.7 g0 g

The reason is straightforward. A date still contains about 21% water, and part of its weight is fiber, protein, and minerals; almost all the weight of granulated sugar is carbohydrate.

A 20-gram comparison is easier to picture

A 20-g portion of dates provides roughly 55 calories, 13 g of sugars, and 1.3 g of fiber. The same 20 g of granulated sugar supplies about 77 calories, 20 g of sugar, and no fiber.

That is a measurable difference. A recipe, however, may not accept a one-for-one weight swap: dates contain water, take up more space, have their own flavor, and do not dissolve like sucrose. Date paste can change moisture and structure, so culinary substitution is rarely exact.

The advantage comes from the whole-food matrix

In an intact date, sugars remain inside plant tissue along with fiber and cellular structure, and the fruit requires chewing. Granulated sugar dissolves readily and provides no fiber.

That makes a whole date nutritionally more complete than eating the same weight of table sugar. It does not make 100 g of dates a light serving: that amount still contains about 277 calories and more than 66 g of sugars.

“Sweetened with dates” does not guarantee low sugar

A muffin can replace sucrose with a large amount of date paste and still end up very sweet and calorie-dense. To know what changed, you need the amount of dates used plus the rest of the recipe.

Format matters too. One or two whole dates retain a recognizable food matrix; concentrated date syrup behaves much more like other liquid sweeteners in both use and sugar density.

Which makes more sense?

If you want dried fruit, fiber, and the date's flavor and texture, dates clearly offer more than table sugar. If the goal is simply to add sweetness, either ingredient can add substantial sugar and calories depending on the amount.

Dates win as a food, not as permission to sweeten without limits. An equal-weight swap can raise fiber and lower sugar, but the final result depends on how many grams actually go into the recipe.

faq.question: Do dates have less sugar than white sugar?
faq.answer: At the same weight, yes. Medjools have about 66–67 g of sugars per 100 g, while granulated sugar is about 100 g of sugar per 100 g.

faq.question: Are dates lower in calories than sugar?
faq.answer: At equal weight, yes: about 277 calories per 100 g versus about 387. A recipe may use different amounts, so a date substitution does not automatically lower calories.

faq.question: Is it better to sweeten with dates?
faq.answer: Whole dates provide fiber and minerals that table sugar does not. They are still concentrated in sugars, so the benefit depends on portion size and whether you use whole fruit, paste, or syrup.
